legacy_conversion_note: The original docx (source/Y1/Session 3/College Admissions/Case Study_ College Admissions.docx) presents Jack Ygarret, Betsy Peterson, Zach Laursen, and the two applicants Tisha Ackerman and Harrison Carter as a real Stanford admissions committee deciding a real 2020-2021 admissions cycle. No public record ties named individuals to a real Stanford admissions committee, and this conversion does not claim these five people or this specific committee meeting are real -- they are kept as the original case's own fictional framing device (an admissions-committee decision scenario), the same way A Coach's Dilemma keeps its invented coach and players. What IS real and independently verified in this conversion: Stanford University's Common Data Set is a real, annually published institutional report (sources[] S1-S4), and Appendix A's figures (57,326 applicants, 2,067 admitted, SAT/ACT 25th-75th percentile bounds, average GPA, percent with 4.0 GPA, percent in top-tenth class rank) are the most recent published edition's real numbers -- replacing the original docx's stale 2019-2020 Common Data Set PDF (source/Y1/Session 3/College Admissions/stanford-cds-2019-A.pdf), which reported Fall 2019 enrollment and is 6+ admissions cycles out of date as of this conversion (2026-08-17). The legacy PDF was read in full and its own real 2019-2020 figures (SAT 1440-1550, 24,902+22,596=47,498 applicants, 987+1,075=2,062 admitted) are NOT reused in case.md -- they are superseded by the fresher, currently reachable Appendix A figures, consistent with case-write's stale-figure-update instruction. Tisha Ackerman's and Harrison Carter's individual application data (SAT/ACT breakdown, GPA, AP scores, class rank percentile, extracurriculars, essay excerpts) are kept verbatim from the legacy docx as the case's own given, internally self-consistent applicant dataset -- the same treatment A Coach's Dilemma gives its player box-score numbers, i.e. a word problem's own stated data does not require an external citation. The legacy Appendix B (a claimed roster of real 'Stanford University 2020-2021 Applicants Rejected/Admitted') was NOT carried into this conversion -- it named no actual students and provided no reproducible data, only a stub with no table, so keeping it would have created either an orphan appendix or a fabricated one. Appendix B was repurposed instead to hold a real, sourced U.S. average public-high-school-enrollment figure (NCES-derived, sources[] S5-S6), needed because Harrison Carter's application states his school type only as 'Public' with no enrollment figure -- a genuine data gap in the original legacy material, not something this conversion invented.

modeling_assumptions.text: This case's committee scene (Jack Ygarret, Betsy Peterson, Zach Laursen) and the specific pairing of Tisha Ackerman vs. Harrison Carter as finalists for one open spot are fiction, kept from the original case materials (see legacy_conversion_note). Stanford's institutional Common Data Set figures in Appendix A are real and independently sourced (sources[] S1-S4).

D5 converts each applicant's stated class-rank percentile into an estimated raw count of classmates who rank above them, which requires knowing the applicant's high school enrollment. Tisha's application states her school's size directly (3,200+ students). Harrison's application states only 'Public' with no enrollment figure, so this case substitutes the U.S. national average public high school enrollment (Appendix B, derived from sources[] S5) as a stated stand-in. This is a real simplification: an individual school's actual size can differ substantially from the national average, and the case's answer is sensitive to this substitution (see FACILITATOR.md and sensitivity_model.py) -- the direction and size of that sensitivity are not stated here.

Comparing 'class rank percentile' between two different high schools assumes both schools compute rank the same way (typically unweighted or weighted GPA-based rank). Real high schools vary in ranking methodology and in whether they rank at all; this case does not adjust for that variation, since neither application states its school's ranking method.

D1's box-and-whisker plot uses Stanford's published 25th and 75th percentile SAT Composite bounds (Appendix A) as the box edges. Stanford's Common Data Set does not publish a raw median SAT score, so the median line on the box plot is estimated as the midpoint of the 25th/75th bounds -- a modeling simplification, not a reported Stanford statistic.

deliverables.text: A box-and-whisker plot of Stanford's admitted-class SAT Composite range (Appendix A), with both applicants' SAT Composite scores marked on it, stating whether either falls outside the box.
An original scatter plot comparing Tisha and Harrison across at least two quantitative measures, plotted against Stanford's published class benchmarks (Appendix A).
A data table citing at least 5 data points from Stanford's Common Data Set (Appendix A) supporting the chosen position, with each applicant's corresponding number placed next to it.
A computed comparison of Tisha's and Harrison's SAT Composite scores: the point gap between them, and that gap expressed as a percentage of the lower score.

A raw-count estimate, for each applicant, of how many classmates rank above them at their own high school, using their stated class-rank percentile and their high school's enrollment (given for Tisha; a stated national-average assumption for Harrison), with the assumption written out.

balance.argument_a: Tisha Ackerman's unweighted GPA (3.73) beats Harrison's (3.69), and her stated class-rank percentile (3rd) is numerically better than his (7th). She is a first-generation college student from a lower-income background, a profile Stanford's own published data on rank and background says the committee actively weighs, and her AP scores in Physics C Mechanics and English Lang are both perfect 5s in a rigorous course load.
balance.argument_b: Harrison Carter's SAT Composite (1520) and ACT Composite (34) both beat Tisha's (1480 / 32) and sit closer to -- in the ACT's case, inside -- Stanford's published middle-50% admitted range (Appendix A). He took more AP exams (6 vs. 4) with a higher average score (4.83 vs. 4.5), including three perfect 5s, is requesting financial aid, and holds a concrete technical credential (an Intel apprenticeship) directly relevant to his stated major.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric: the point gap between Tisha's and Harrison's SAT Composite scores (Appendix C/D), expressed as a percentage of the lower score -- directly one of the case's own required deliverables (D4). See derived{} for the worked figures.
balance.stability: The graded primary metric (SAT Composite point gap) does not depend on any stated assumption -- both scores are given, verbatim, in the applicants' own application files, so it is stable by construction and is not exercised by probe 5's flex sweep at all. The case's disclosed secondary comparison (D5's raw-count-above estimate) DOES depend on a stated assumption (MA2, Harrison's substituted national-average school enrollment, ~649 students) and probe 5 flexes it +/-50% (see sensitivity_model.py). Across that full range the comparison's direction does not flip -- Harrison's estimated headcount-above stays lower than Tisha's fixed 96 at every flex point -- but the size of the gap moves substantially (roughly a 3x range across the swept enrollment values), which is itself a real, disclosed limitation: the conclusion is directionally robust to a plausible range of school-size error, but the exact margin is not a fact, it is an estimate resting on a national average standing in for one specific, unstated school. See sensitivity_model.py's printed flex sweep and FACILITATOR.md's sensitivity note for the full disclosed reveal.

sensitivity_note: A college-admissions decision case with no illness/death/money-stress/family-hardship content beyond ordinary financial-aid/income-bracket data already present in each applicant's own file. The one real sensitivity: D5's raw-count-above comparison depends on a stated national-average school-size assumption for Harrison (MA2), since his application does not state his school's enrollment -- this is a genuine, disclosed modeling limitation, not a flaw to paper over. See FACILITATOR.md's sensitivity note and SPEC.md Section 6.

cohort_bands.note: The room typically splits early on GPA/rank (favoring Tisha) vs. test scores (favoring Harrison); D5's school-size reveal is the moment that usually produces an audible reaction once the raw counts are computed and compared.

D1's box-and-whisker plot is built once as a shared example, then each pair completes D2-D5 independently; D5's assumption-writing step is worth doing as a full-group discussion before pairs finalize their own numbers.
